title: Software Engineer (DSA and interviews)
summary: Software engineers design, write and fix code that other people rely on. Many software hiring processes include coding problems on data structures and algorithms. This path suits students who enjoy problem solving and want to be ready for coding rounds and technical interviews.

sources.title: Programming, Data Structures and Algorithms Using Python – NPTEL
Preparing to Interview and Interviewing – The Odin Project

nodes.title: One language, written fluently
nodes.summary: Pick one of Python, Java or C++ and stick with it. Get comfortable with loops, functions, strings, arrays or lists, maps and classes, so the language never slows you down when you are solving a problem.

resources.title: CS50's Introduction to Programming with Python

nodes.proof: Solve the first 20 introductory problems on the CSES Problem Set in your chosen language without looking up syntax.

nodes.title: Big-O and complexity analysis
nodes.summary: Learn to estimate how fast a solution runs and how much memory it uses as the input grows. Interviewers expect you to state the time and space cost of your answer and to compare it with other approaches.
nodes.proof: For ten of your past solutions, write the time and space complexity in a comment and explain one faster or smaller alternative.

nodes.title: Arrays, hashing, stacks, queues and linked lists
nodes.summary: These basic data structures appear in most coding problems. Learn how each one works inside, what each operation costs, and when to choose one over another. Hash tables in particular turn many slow solutions into fast ones.

resources.title: Programming, Data Structures and Algorithms Using Python – NPTEL

nodes.proof: Implement a stack, a queue, a singly linked list and a simple hash map from scratch, each with a few unit tests, in a public Git repo.

sources.title: Programming, Data Structures and Algorithms Using Python – NPTEL

nodes.title: Sorting, searching and recursion
nodes.summary: Understand merge sort, quick sort and heap sort, binary search, and how to think recursively. Many harder problems are really a sorting or binary search idea in disguise, so practise spotting them.

resources.title: Programming, Data Structures and Algorithms Using Python – NPTEL

nodes.proof: Write merge sort, quick sort and binary search yourself, then solve ten CSES problems that need sorting or binary search.

nodes.title: Trees, heaps and graphs
nodes.summary: Learn binary trees, binary search trees and heaps, then graphs: breadth-first and depth-first search and shortest paths. These topics come up often in interviews and model real things like maps, networks and dependencies.

resources.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms – NPTEL

nodes.proof: Solve 15 tree and graph problems on CSES, including at least one shortest-path problem, and explain each approach in a short note.

sources.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms – NPTEL

nodes.title: Greedy algorithms and dynamic programming
nodes.summary: Greedy methods make the best local choice; dynamic programming breaks a problem into overlapping subproblems and reuses answers. Both feel hard at first and get easier with steady practice on classic problems.

resources.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms – NPTEL

nodes.proof: Solve ten dynamic programming problems on CSES and, for each, write down the state, the transition and the base case.

sources.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms – NPTEL

nodes.title: Steady problem-solving practice
nodes.summary: Knowing the topics is not enough; you need speed and calm under a time limit. Solve problems regularly across all topics, keep notes on mistakes, and revisit problems you could not solve after a few days.
nodes.proof: A log of 150 or more solved problems across topics, with a one-line note on the key idea for each.

nodes.title: CS fundamentals: OOP, databases, OS and networks
nodes.summary: Technical interviews for freshers often go beyond coding problems into object-oriented design, SQL and database basics, operating system ideas like processes and memory, and how the web and HTTP work. Revise the core ideas from your coursework.

resources.title: CS50's Introduction to Databases with SQL (archived, free to view)
Overview of HTTP – MDN Web Docs
The Missing Semester of Your CS Education – MIT

nodes.proof: Write one page of your own revision notes per subject and answer them aloud to a friend without reading.

nodes.title: Build and ship one real project
nodes.summary: Employers want to see that you can build and ship working software, not only solve puzzles. Build one small but complete project, keep it on GitHub with a clear README, and be ready to explain your design choices.
nodes.proof: A public GitHub repo with a README, setup steps, screenshots or a demo, and a commit history that shows steady work.

sources.title: What You Can Do to Prepare – The Odin Project

nodes.title: Mock interviews and job search
nodes.summary: Practise explaining your thinking aloud while you code, because interviewers judge how you reason as well as the final answer. Learn the usual hiring steps, prepare your resume, and apply steadily rather than all at once.

resources.title: Preparing to Interview and Interviewing – The Odin Project
What Companies Want – The Odin Project

nodes.proof: Complete five timed mock interviews with classmates or seniors, and keep notes on what to improve after each one.
